title: Part 3: the discussion
summary: After this unit you can discuss abstract and speculative questions with clear reasons, examples, careful hedging and accurate comparisons across time.

items.title: What changes in Part 3
body: Part 3 lasts four to five minutes and moves from your personal story in Part 2 to general, abstract questions on the same theme: society, trends, comparisons, causes, the future. The examiner is now testing whether you can **discuss ideas**, not just describe experiences.

The examiner may challenge you, ask you to compare, or push you to speculate. This is not a sign you are doing badly; it is how they find your ceiling. Band 9 candidates handle these questions with developed, well-reasoned answers of 30-60 seconds.
list: Opinion: *Do you think older people have less to teach the young than in the past?*
Comparison: *How is learning different now from your parents' generation?*
Speculation: *How might tourism change over the next twenty years?*
Cause and effect: *Why do some people find it harder to be patient nowadays?*
Evaluation: *Is it better to learn a skill from a teacher or by yourself?*

items.title: Giving reasons and examples
body: A developed answer usually has three moves: a clear position, a reason, and an example or consequence. Then you can add a qualification (*That said...*) to show you can see complexity.
Move from the general to the specific and back again. A short concrete example (*my own parents, for instance...*) makes an abstract point convincing, but don't let it turn into another Part 2 story.

examples.text: I think they still have a great deal to teach, but perhaps not in the areas we traditionally assumed. Technical knowledge goes out of date quickly, so a grandparent probably can't teach you much about computers. What they can offer is perspective: they've lived through several economic crises, for instance, and that tends to make them much calmer about setbacks than younger people are.

items.title: Hedging and speculation
body: Abstract questions rarely have certain answers, so careful speakers hedge. Hedging is not weakness; at band 9 it shows precision about how sure you are.
list: **Tentative opinion**: *I'd say*, *I suspect*, *My sense is that*, *I tend to think*
**Probability**: *It's quite likely that*, *There's a good chance*, *I doubt whether*
**Generalising carefully**: *on the whole*, *by and large*, *in many cases*, *to some extent*
**Speculating about the future**: *I can imagine a situation where*, *It wouldn't surprise me if*, *We may well see*
items.tip: Don't stack hedges (*maybe perhaps it might possibly be*). One well-chosen hedge per claim is enough.

items.title: Comparing past, present and future; buying time
body: Many Part 3 questions invite comparison across time. Mix tenses accurately: *used to* and *would* for the past, present perfect for change up to now (*has become*), present simple for general truths, and modal or future forms for speculation.
When you need a moment to think, use natural phrases that sound like genuine reflection, not stock fillers. Never say *That's a good question* to every question: it becomes a tic.

examples.text: Hmm, I haven't really thought about that before, but...
That's a difficult one. I suppose it depends on...
Well, if you'd asked me ten years ago I'd have said..., but now...
examples.note: Buys time and sets up a time comparison.

items.q: Q: 'Why do you think some people prefer to learn skills from videos rather than from a teacher?' Which answer is best developed?
options: Videos are good and teachers are also good. Both have advantages.

I suspect cost is a big part of it, since an online tutorial is usually free, but flexibility matters too: you can pause, rewind and practise at two in the morning if you want to. That said, I think people sometimes underestimate what they lose, which is someone who can spot their mistakes.
That's a good question. That's a very good question. I think people like videos.
items.why: C gives two reasons with explanation and a qualification. A is undeveloped, B says nothing specific, and D relies on fillers.

items.q: Choose the function of each phrase.

rows.label: It wouldn't surprise me if more cities banned short-term rentals.
I tend to think young people are more patient than we give them credit for.
Hmm, that's a tricky one. Let me think...
That said, it's not true in every case.
We may well see a return to more local holidays.
By and large, people seem happier when they travel more slowly.

items.why: Speculation looks forward with modals or *it wouldn't surprise me if*; hedges soften a claim; time-buying phrases are honest pauses; qualifications limit a claim you have just made.

items.text: Q: 'Has tourism changed in your country?' A: 'Enormously. People ___ to go to the same beach every summer, whereas now they want something different every year.'
items.why: *Used to* (or *tended to*) contrasts a past habit with the present.

items.text: Over the last twenty years, the way people book holidays ___ changed almost beyond recognition.
items.why: Present perfect (*has changed*) for change over a period continuing up to now (*over the last twenty years*).

items.text: I ___ whether people will ever travel as much as they did before; the costs are rising too quickly.
items.why: *I doubt whether* is a natural way to express low probability; *I question whether* is a slightly more sceptical alternative.

options: All young people are impatient. Everyone knows this.
Maybe perhaps possibly some young people might be a bit impatient, perhaps.
I'd say young people are, on the whole, less used to waiting, simply because so much is available instantly, but I don't think that makes them inherently less patient.
items.why: C uses one hedge (*I'd say*, *on the whole*) for each claim and then distinguishes habit from character. A and D overgeneralise; B stacks hedges until the answer means nothing.

items.q: The examiner asks a question you have never thought about. What should you do?
options: Acknowledge it naturally, then reason your way to a position aloud.
Say 'I don't know' and wait for the next question.
Switch to a topic you have prepared.
Repeat the question word for word slowly.
items.why: Thinking aloud with natural markers (*I haven't really considered that, but I suppose...*) shows exactly the flexible, extended discourse examiners want.

questions: Do you think older people have as much to teach young people as they did in the past?
How much contact do young people in your country have with older generations?
Can older people learn from younger people too?
Do you think housing schemes that bring old and young people together will become more common?
What could be done to encourage more learning between generations?

text: I think they still have a great deal to teach, but perhaps not in the areas we traditionally assumed. Technical knowledge dates very quickly, so my grandfather couldn't teach me much about software. What older people can offer is perspective: they've lived through crises and changes that we've only read about, and that often makes them far calmer about setbacks. There's also something they can teach about relationships: how to keep a friendship going for fifty years, or how to put things right after an argument. That kind of wisdom doesn't come up in a search engine, and I think young people underestimate how much they could learn just by asking.

Hmm, I'd say less than they used to. In the past, families tended to live closer together, and children would spend a lot of time with grandparents almost by default. Now people move for work, so those everyday conversations happen over a video call once a week, if at all, and a lot of that informal learning gets lost. That said, it varies a lot. In smaller towns, where families haven't spread out so much, you still see grandparents doing the school run every day, and those children probably spend more time with older relatives than with anyone apart from their parents.

Definitely, and I think it's underrated. Both my parents learnt to use their phones properly from my younger brother, not from any course. And it can be good for the relationship, because it reverses the usual roles for a moment, which I suspect both sides quite enjoy. Beyond technology, younger people can also make older relatives rethink some of their attitudes, about mental health, for example, or about what counts as a proper job. It doesn't always go smoothly, but when it works, both generations come away with a slightly broader view of the world.

It wouldn't surprise me if they became more common. Some cities already have schemes where students live rent-free with older people in exchange for company and a bit of help around the house. That kind of arrangement seems to solve two problems at once: loneliness and housing costs. Of course, it depends on finding the right people. Not every student wants to spend their evenings chatting, and not every older person wants a stranger in the house. But with careful matching, and perhaps some support from the council, I can see it spreading, especially in cities where rents keep rising.

That's a difficult one. I suppose schools could do more, but I'm wary of turning everything into a formal programme. The best intergenerational learning tends to happen when people are doing something together, cooking or fixing something, rather than when someone sets out to teach. So rather than adding lessons, I'd create more shared spaces: community gardens, repair cafés, choirs where teenagers and pensioners actually mix. Once people are working side by side, the conversation tends to take care of itself, and the learning happens almost without anyone noticing, which is probably why it sticks.
notes: Each answer opens with a clear position and develops it with a reason and a concrete example.
Time comparisons are handled with precise grammar (*would spend*, *used to*, *Now people move*).
Hedging and speculation are natural and varied (*I'd say*, *I suspect*, *It wouldn't surprise me if*, *I'm wary of*).
Time-buying phrases (*Hmm*, *That's a difficult one. I suppose...*) sound like genuine thought and lead straight into an answer.
Abstract vocabulary is used precisely (*perspective*, *intergenerational learning*, *reverses the usual roles*).
Each answer runs to roughly 90-120 words, about 40-45 seconds at a natural pace: long enough to develop a position with a reason, an example and a qualification, short enough to stay a conversation.

phrases: perhaps not in the areas we traditionally assumed

questions: Why do you think famous tourist sites are sometimes disappointing?
Is tourism always good for the places people visit?
How do you think tourism will change in the future?
How are holidays different now from in your parents' generation?
Why do some people prefer to visit unusual places?

text: I think social media has a lot to do with it. People see the same five photographs of a place before they go, so they arrive wanting to recreate them, and they end up queueing for a picture rather than actually looking around. Less famous places don't come with that baggage, so you experience them more on their own terms. There's also the problem of expectations. If you've been told all your life that a building is one of the wonders of the world, it would be hard for anything to live up to that, especially when you're seeing it over the heads of three hundred other people.

Mostly, but not always. It brings money and jobs, obviously, but in some cities it's pushed rents up so far that locals can no longer afford to live in the centre. I'd say it's positive as long as the numbers are managed, and that's the hard part. There's an environmental cost too. Popular beaches and mountain paths can be badly damaged by sheer numbers of feet, and Venice has started charging day-trippers a fee on its busiest days. So I'd say the real question isn't whether tourism is good or bad, but how much a place can absorb.

I suspect we'll see a shift towards slower, more local travel, partly because of cost and partly because people are more aware of the environmental impact of flying. Having said that, people have been predicting the end of cheap flights for years, and it hasn't happened yet, so I wouldn't bet on it. One thing I'm fairly confident about is booking. I imagine more popular sites will use timed tickets, the way some museums already do, simply to control the crowds, and that could actually make visits more pleasant, even if it takes away some of the spontaneity.

In my parents' day, a holiday was a fixed event: the same place, the same two weeks every year, booked months in advance through an agent. Now it's much more spontaneous. People book a weekend away on their phone on a Thursday night. There's more choice, but I'm not sure people relax as much. My parents also say that being away meant being genuinely out of contact: no emails, no messages, just a postcard home. Now most people check their phones on the beach, so although we travel more often, I suspect we switch off less than they did.

I think it's partly about curiosity and partly about status, if I'm honest. Saying you've been somewhere unusual has become a kind of social currency, whereas a generation ago just going abroad was impressive in itself. There's a practical side as well. Unusual places tend to be cheaper and less crowded, and you're more likely to meet local people than other tourists. Personally, some of my best trips have been to towns I'd never even heard of before I arrived, precisely because I went there with no expectations at all.
notes: The answers combine personal perspective with general analysis, never slipping back into Part 2 storytelling.
Balanced evaluation (*Mostly, but not always*; *as long as*) shows the ability to discuss complexity.
Future speculation is hedged and then challenged (*Having said that... I wouldn't bet on it*), a sophisticated discourse move.
Idiomatic language suits the spoken register (*come with that baggage*, *on their own terms*, *social currency*).
Past-present comparison is clear and grammatically accurate.
Each answer runs to roughly 90-120 words, about 40-45 seconds at a natural pace: long enough to develop a position with a reason, an example and a qualification, short enough to stay a conversation.

phrases: has a lot to do with it
as long as the numbers are managed

questions: Is it better to learn a skill from a teacher or by yourself?
What is the hardest part of teaching yourself something?
How has the internet changed the way people learn new skills?
Should schools spend more time teaching students how to learn?
Do you think qualifications will become less important in the future?

text: It depends on the skill. For something practical like coding or cooking, the internet probably has everything you need. But for anything where small errors become bad habits, a musical instrument, say, or a sport, I think a teacher is worth a great deal, because they can see things you can't see yourself. For a lot of people, the best answer is probably a mixture: a few lessons at the start to get the basics right, then practising on your own with the occasional check-up. That way you avoid the bad habits without paying for years of classes.

Motivation, mainly. When you're paying a teacher and someone's expecting you on Tuesday, you turn up. When it's just you and a video, it's very easy to tell yourself you'll do it tomorrow, and tomorrow never comes. The other difficulty is knowing whether you're actually improving. Without someone to tell you, it's easy either to stay at the same level for months without realising it, or to give up because you think you're getting nowhere. I find that small, measurable targets help, like being able to play one particular piece by the end of the month.

Hugely. My parents would have needed a library, a class or someone who knew how to do it. Now you can learn almost anything for free, at any hour. The downside is the sheer quantity: knowing which source to trust has become a skill in itself. It's also changed people's sense of how long learning takes. People expect to pick up a skill from a ten-minute video, and for some things that works, but deeper skills still take months of practice. I think some people get discouraged when they discover that the internet can't shorten that part.

Partly, yes. I think schools are still quite focused on content, whereas the most useful thing they could teach is how to learn: how to practise, how to deal with frustration, how to check your own progress. Those habits outlast any particular subject. At the moment, many students only find out how to study effectively at university, or never at all. If they learnt early on, at secondary school, say, how memory works and why cramming the night before an exam is so ineffective, I think they'd do better in every subject, not just one.

I'd like to think so. Employers are already starting to care more about what you can do than where you learnt it, and that would probably accelerate if there were reliable ways of testing skills directly. Whether traditional qualifications disappear, though, I doubt it. They're too embedded. In some fields, like medicine or law, I'd actually be worried if qualifications mattered less, because the public needs a guarantee of competence. But in creative or technical work, I can easily imagine a portfolio of what you've actually made becoming at least as important as a certificate.
notes: Answers are qualified with *It depends* followed by a precise distinction, which is far stronger than a vague 'it depends'.
Reasoning is explicit and causal (*because they can see things you can't*, *When... When...*).
A second conditional and a past modal (*would have needed*) appear naturally in comparison and speculation.
Abstract nouns are well controlled (*motivation*, *quantity*, *habits outlast any particular subject*).
The final answer combines optimism with doubt, showing nuanced speculation.
Each answer runs to roughly 90-120 words, about 40-45 seconds at a natural pace: long enough to develop a position with a reason, an example and a qualification, short enough to stay a conversation.

questions: Do you think people are less patient than they used to be?
How can parents teach children to be patient?
Has technology made us better or worse at waiting?
What kinds of jobs require the most patience?
Will people become even less patient in the future?

text: I'd say we're less used to waiting rather than less patient by nature. When films, food and information all arrive instantly, any delay feels unusual, so it's more irritating. But put people in a situation where waiting is normal, like fishing or gardening, and many of them are perfectly patient. I'd also say patience depends a lot on whether we can see a reason for the delay. If a train is late and nobody explains why, people get angry very quickly, but if the driver announces a signal failure, most passengers just sigh and wait.

Mostly through example, I think. Children watch how adults react to queues and delays. If a parent loses their temper every time a website is slow, the child learns that waiting is a kind of injustice. I suppose activities with a slow payoff, learning an instrument or growing plants, can help as well. Another thing that helps, I think, is not filling every spare moment with a screen. If a child is handed a tablet the moment they're bored in a restaurant, they never get the chance to find out that boredom passes, or that they can entertain themselves.

Both, in a way. Technology has removed a lot of pointless waiting, like queueing at the bank, and that's a genuine improvement. The risk is that we lose the ability to tolerate the waiting that can't be removed, like recovering from an illness or building a career. And on a smaller scale, phones mean we never just sit with a delay any more. Ten minutes at a bus stop used to be a chance to think; now we fill it automatically, which probably makes the waiting feel easier but leaves us less practised at it.

Probably jobs where results take years to appear: scientific research, teaching, medicine to some extent. A teacher may never see what becomes of most of their students, which must require a particular kind of patience. Caring jobs come to mind as well, like nursing or looking after people with dementia, where you might have to answer the same question many times a day and still stay calm and kind. To be honest, I think that kind of patience is seriously undervalued, considering how hard it must be to keep it up day after day, often for quite low pay.

I suspect so, though not necessarily in a bad way. Services will keep getting faster, so expectations will keep rising. But it wouldn't surprise me if there was a counter-movement too; you can already see it in the popularity of things like slow cooking and long walking holidays. And I think younger people in particular are starting to notice that constant speed has a cost. Some of my friends deliberately leave their phones at home at weekends, which would have seemed odd ten years ago, so I'm not convinced the trend only goes one way.
notes: The first answer reframes the question with a precise distinction (*less used to waiting rather than less patient by nature*), a hallmark of band 9 discussion.
Examples are brief and illustrative rather than full stories, which keeps the focus on general ideas.
Concession and contrast are handled smoothly (*Both, in a way... The risk is that...*).
Speculation is careful and two-sided, ending with a supported prediction (*you can already see it in...*).
Natural, precise collocations: *lose their temper*, *a slow payoff*, *tolerate the waiting*, *a counter-movement*.
Each answer runs to roughly 90-120 words, about 40-45 seconds at a natural pace: long enough to develop a position with a reason, an example and a qualification, short enough to stay a conversation.

phrases: less used to X rather than less Y by nature
